title: Chemists Make the First Modern Medicines
summary: Discover how synthetic chemistry and hormone research produced aspirin, sedatives, Salvarsan and insulin.

lessons.title: Adrenaline: Takamine and the First Isolated Hormone (1901)

levels.kid:
When you get a big scare, your heart pounds and you suddenly feel fast and strong. That is a chemical messenger called **adrenaline** at work. It comes from two small glands that sit on top of your kidneys, like little hats.

Long ago, scientists knew these glands made something powerful. But it was mixed up with lots of other stuff, like a few grains of sugar hidden in a bucket of sand.

In 1900 and 1901, a Japanese chemist in New York named **Jokichi Takamine** and his helper **Keizo Uenaka** finally pulled the messenger out pure, as tiny crystals. It was the first hormone ever made pure!

Doctors soon used it to slow bleeding during surgery and to help people who could not breathe well.
levels.hs:
A **hormone** is a chemical messenger made by a gland and carried in the blood to act on distant organs. **Adrenaline** (called **epinephrine** in the US) is made in the **adrenal medulla**, the inner core of the adrenal glands that sit on top of the kidneys. It drives the **fight-or-flight response**: faster heartbeat, narrowed blood vessels in the skin, wider airways, and more sugar released into the blood.

The discovery happened in steps:
- **1894-95**: George Oliver and Edward Schäfer in London injected adrenal gland extract into animals and saw blood pressure shoot up. Something powerful was in there.
- **1897**: John Jacob Abel at Johns Hopkins made a partly purified chemical form and named it "epinephrine."
- **1900-01**: Jokichi Takamine, working in New York with his assistant Keizo Uenaka, isolated the pure substance as crystals. It was the first hormone ever isolated in pure form. The drug company **Parke-Davis** sold it under the brand name **Adrenalin**.
- **1904**: Friedrich Stolz made adrenaline from scratch in the lab, the first hormone to be chemically synthesized.

Because "Adrenalin" was a trademark, US references adopted "epinephrine" as the official name. Today epinephrine is the first-line emergency treatment for **anaphylaxis**, a life-threatening allergic reaction, which is why people with severe allergies carry autoinjectors.
levels.college:
Adrenaline is a **catecholamine**: a catechol ring (benzene with two adjacent hydroxyl groups) attached to an amine side chain. It is made by **chromaffin cells** of the adrenal medulla, which in humans release mostly adrenaline along with some noradrenaline.

**Biosynthesis** runs from the amino acid tyrosine:
- Tyrosine to L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step)
- L-DOPA to dopamine (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase)
- Dopamine to noradrenaline (dopamine beta-hydroxylase)
- Noradrenaline to adrenaline (**PNMT**, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, which adds a methyl group)

It is cleared quickly by reuptake and by the enzymes **COMT** and **MAO**, so its effects last only minutes.

**Why isolation was hard.** The gland contains only small amounts, and the catechol group **oxidizes easily** in air and light, turning solutions pink and then brown. Takamine and Uenaka concentrated aqueous extracts of animal adrenal glands, removed proteins, and added ammonia, which made the free base precipitate as crystals. At Parke-Davis, Thomas Bell Aldrich independently purified it in 1901 and determined the correct formula, C9H13NO3. Takamine patented the process and licensed it to Parke-Davis.

**Effects** come from adrenergic receptors:
- alpha-1: blood vessel constriction
- beta-1: faster, stronger heartbeat
- beta-2: airway relaxation and glycogen breakdown

**Early uses** followed fast. Surgeons applied it to stop oozing from small vessels by **vasoconstriction**. In 1903 Heinrich Braun added it to cocaine for local anesthesia. The narrowed vessels kept the anesthetic in place longer, a "chemical tourniquet." Injected adrenaline was also used for asthma attacks within a few years.

The chronology is notable. Adrenaline was isolated before the word **hormone** existed: Ernest Starling coined the term in 1905, after he and William Bayliss discovered secretin in 1902.
levels.phd:
The isolation of adrenaline is a case study in priority, chemistry and the birth of receptor pharmacology.

**Priority dispute.** Abel's "epinephrine" (1897-99) was a benzoyl derivative, produced during his purification, that had much weaker activity than the gland extract. In Vienna, Otto von Fürth's "suprarenin" was an impure, iron-containing preparation. Takamine had visited Abel's Baltimore laboratory before announcing his result. Abel later implied that Takamine had borrowed his approach, but Takamine's ammonia-precipitation route differed, and the crystals were the free base, not a derivative. Uenaka's July 1900 notebook, rediscovered decades later, documents the crystallization and highlights the assistant's underappreciated role.

**Stereochemistry.** Stolz's 1904 synthesis (Hoechst; Dakin independently around 1905) gave racemic material. Natural adrenaline is the single levorotatory (R) enantiomer. Flächer resolved the racemate with tartaric acid in 1908, and Arthur Cushny showed the levo form to be markedly more potent than the dextro form. This was among the earliest proofs that biological targets discriminate three-dimensional shape. Easson and Stedman (1933) later explained it with a **three-point attachment** model: the beta-hydroxyl lines up with a receptor binding point in only one enantiomer.

**From hormone to receptor.** In 1904 Thomas Elliott proposed that sympathetic nerves release an adrenaline-like substance, an early statement of chemical neurotransmission. Henry Dale (1906) found that ergot alkaloids reversed adrenaline's pressor effect into a fall in blood pressure, hinting at opposing receptor populations. Raymond Ahlquist (1948) formalized **alpha and beta adrenoceptors** from rank orders of agonist potency.

**Signal transduction.** Earl Sutherland, studying how adrenaline triggers glycogen breakdown in liver, found that it worked in broken-cell preparations through a heat-stable intermediate, **cyclic AMP**. This founded the **second messenger** concept (Nobel 1971). In 2007 Brian Kobilka's group solved the crystal structure of the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor. Kobilka and Robert Lefkowitz shared the 2012 Chemistry Nobel. A molecule crystallized in 1900 ended up anchoring the structural biology of the largest drug-target family.
levels.expert:
Adrenaline also shaped patent law. In **Parke-Davis v. H.K. Mulford (1911)**, Judge Learned Hand upheld Takamine's patent. He reasoned that the purified substance was "for every practical purpose a new thing commercially and therapeutically." For a century that logic supported patents on isolated natural products. In **Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics (2013)**, the US Supreme Court held that isolating naturally occurring DNA did not make it patent-eligible. That decision narrowed the principle that isolation by itself creates a new invention.

**Clinical realities today:**
- **Anaphylaxis**: intramuscular epinephrine is first-line, and antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not substitutes. Delayed or omitted epinephrine is a recurring factor in fatal cases. Autoinjectors reached the US market in 1987, and in 2024 the FDA approved the first epinephrine nasal spray (neffy), aimed at people who hesitate to use needles.
- **Cardiac arrest**: the PARAMEDIC2 trial (NEJM, 2018) found that epinephrine improved 30-day survival after out-of-hospital arrest but did not significantly improve survival with a favorable neurological outcome. More survivors had severe brain injury. One hypothesis is that strong alpha-mediated vasoconstriction restores coronary perfusion while impairing cerebral microcirculation. The best timing and total exposure remain open questions.
- **Labeling errors**: ratio-style concentration labels led to repeated mix-ups between formulations. Around 2016, US labeling moved to mass-per-volume expressions.

**Pitfalls relevant to neurosurgery:**
- Local anesthetic with epinephrine is widely used in scalp infiltration to reduce bleeding. However, systemic absorption can cause tachycardia and hypertension, which matters in patients with raised intracranial pressure or aneurysms.
- The teaching that epinephrine must never be used in fingers comes largely from older, acidic procaine preparations. Modern evidence supports its safety in digital blocks, and phentolamine can reverse vasoconstriction.
- Epinephrine is polar and crosses an intact blood-brain barrier poorly, so central symptoms during catecholamine surges are mostly secondary to hemodynamic effects.
- In suspected **pheochromocytoma**, plasma or urine metanephrines (COMT metabolites) are the screening test, because the parent hormone has a short half-life and its levels fluctuate.
- Catecholamine solutions oxidize to adrenochrome, so discolored solutions should be discarded. Sulfite antioxidants in some products raise sensitivity questions, though epinephrine is still given in anaphylaxis.

Parke-Davis sold it as Adrenalin, so the US adopted the name epinephrine

test.q: Who first isolated pure, crystalline adrenaline in 1900-1901?
test.explain: Jokichi Takamine and his assistant Keizo Uenaka crystallized the pure hormone. Oliver and Schäfer had earlier shown that adrenal extract raises blood pressure, but they did not purify it.

test.q: Which part of the body produces adrenaline?
test.explain: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, the inner core of the gland, make adrenaline. The cortex, the outer layer, makes steroid hormones such as cortisol.

test.q: What did Oliver and Schäfer demonstrate in 1894-95?
test.explain: Injecting adrenal extract into animals caused a dramatic rise in blood pressure. This showed that the gland contained a powerful active substance.

test.q: Why is the hormone officially called epinephrine in the United States?
choices: Adrenalin was a registered brand name
Epinephrine refers to the synthetic form

test.q: Who first synthesized adrenaline chemically, in 1904?
test.explain: Stolz at Hoechst made adrenaline from scratch, the first synthesis of a hormone. Aldrich purified it and determined its formula, but he did not synthesize it.

test.q: Surgeons used adrenaline to reduce bleeding because it:
test.explain: Through alpha-1 receptors, adrenaline narrows small vessels (vasoconstriction), which reduces oozing. Relaxing the airways is a real beta-2 effect, but it does not reduce bleeding.

test.q: Why did Heinrich Braun add adrenaline to cocaine for local anesthesia in 1903?
choices: To keep the anesthetic in place longer
To make the injection less painful
To speed up recovery of the nerves
To cancel cocaine's effects on the heart
test.explain: Vasoconstriction slows removal of the anesthetic by the blood, so it acts longer. This is why the technique was called a chemical tourniquet.

test.q: Which enzyme converts noradrenaline into adrenaline?
test.explain: PNMT adds a methyl group to noradrenaline to make adrenaline. COMT and MAO break catecholamines down, and tyrosine hydroxylase acts at the first step of the pathway.

test.q: What made adrenaline difficult to purify from glands?
choices: It is a large, fragile protein
It breaks down when kept cold
test.explain: The catechol ring oxidizes in air and light, and the glands contain only small amounts. Adrenaline is a small molecule, not a protein.

test.q: What word did Ernest Starling coin in 1905 for chemical messengers carried in the blood?
test.explain: Starling introduced the term after he and Bayliss discovered secretin, a few years after adrenaline had already been isolated.

test.q: Takamine licensed his process to the drug company ___, which sold the hormone as Adrenalin.
test.explain: Parke-Davis marketed Adrenalin. Thomas Bell Aldrich, a chemist there, also independently purified the hormone and determined its formula.

test.q: What is the name of the life-threatening allergic reaction for which epinephrine is the first-line treatment?
test.explain: Epinephrine reverses airway narrowing and blood pressure collapse in anaphylaxis, which is why people with severe allergies carry autoinjectors.

advancedTest.q: Cushny found levo-adrenaline markedly more potent than the dextro form. What does this most directly imply?
choices: Synthetic racemates contain toxic side products
The dextro form is cleared more slowly by MAO
Its receptors distinguish the molecule's 3D shape
The dextro form is converted into noradrenaline
advancedTest.explain: Mirror-image molecules with identical chemical composition differ in potency only if the target is stereoselective. The three-point attachment model later explained this.

advancedTest.q: Parke-Davis v. Mulford (1911) upheld a patent on purified adrenaline, but Myriad (2013) rejected patents on isolated genes. Which idea did Myriad reject?
choices: A medical use makes a substance patentable
Isolation alone makes natural products new
advancedTest.explain: Learned Hand treated purification as creating a commercially new thing. Myriad held that isolating a naturally occurring DNA sequence did not by itself make it patent-eligible.

advancedTest.q: PARAMEDIC2 found that epinephrine improved 30-day survival after cardiac arrest without significantly improving favorable neurological outcomes. Which interpretation fits best?
choices: Neurological outcomes improved while survival fell
The drug failed to restart circulation in most cases
Extra survivors were often left with severe brain injury
Epinephrine damaged the heart more than the brain
advancedTest.explain: More patients survived, but a larger share of survivors had severe neurological impairment. One proposed reason is vasoconstriction impairing cerebral microcirculation.

advancedTest.q: Sutherland found that adrenaline triggered liver glycogen breakdown through a heat-stable factor in broken-cell preparations. Why was this conceptually important?
choices: It showed that hormones act directly on glycogen itself
It placed adrenaline's receptors inside the nucleus
It showed hormones can signal through second messengers
It showed the liver inactivates circulating hormones
advancedTest.explain: The factor was cyclic AMP, an intracellular messenger produced after the hormone binds a surface receptor. This founded the second messenger concept.

lessons.title: Aspirin: From Willow Bark to Bayer (1897)

levels.kid:
Long ago, people noticed something special about willow trees. If they chewed the bark or made it into tea, aches and fevers felt a little better. Ancient Egyptians wrote about it. In 1763, a priest in England named Edward Stone tested it on people with fevers.

Later, scientists found the helper chemical hiding inside the bark. They called it **salicin**, after Salix, the Latin word for willow. But medicines made from it tasted awful and upset people's tummies.

In 1897, a chemist named **Felix Hoffmann** worked at a company called **Bayer**. He changed the chemical just a tiny bit, like swapping one Lego brick. The new version was gentler on the tummy. Bayer named it **aspirin**, and it became one of the most famous medicines in the world!
levels.hs:
Aspirin is an **analgesic** (pain reliever), an **antipyretic** (fever reducer) and an **anti-inflammatory**. Its story shows how medicine moved from plants to purified, then redesigned, chemicals.

The path went like this:
- **Willow bark** was used for pain and fever for thousands of years; the Egyptian Ebers Papyrus mentions willow. In 1763 Reverend **Edward Stone** reported to the Royal Society that powdered bark helped 'agues' (fevers).
- In 1828 **Johann Buchner** isolated the active compound, a bitter substance he named **salicin**.
- In 1838 **Raffaele Piria** turned salicin into **salicylic acid**, which turned out to be the real active form.
- In 1859 **Hermann Kolbe** found how to make salicylic acid from coal-tar chemicals, so it became cheap.

Doctors soon used salicylic acid and its salt, sodium salicylate, to treat **rheumatic fever** and arthritis. The problem: it irritated the stomach and tasted terrible.

On 10 August 1897, **Felix Hoffmann**, a chemist at the German company **Bayer**, attached an **acetyl group** to salicylic acid, making pure, stable **acetylsalicylic acid**. Bayer registered the name **Aspirin** in 1899: 'a' for acetyl, 'spir' for Spiraea (meadowsweet, another plant source of salicylates), and '-in', a common ending for drug names. It was gentler to take, and it became one of the first mass-produced synthetic drugs.
levels.college:
Aspirin's history runs through three chemical steps: isolation, conversion, and deliberate modification.

**From plant to compound.** Salicin is a glucoside: salicyl alcohol (saligenin) bonded to glucose. In the body it acts as a **prodrug**: gut enzymes remove the sugar and the liver oxidizes the alcohol to **salicylic acid**. Piria performed this conversion in the lab in 1838; Karl Löwig independently got related acids from meadowsweet (Spiraea ulmaria) in 1835.

**Cheap synthesis.** Kolbe's 1859 route (refined into the **Kolbe-Schmitt reaction**) made salicylic acid from phenol and carbon dioxide. The von Heyden company industrialized it in 1874. In 1876 Thomas MacLagan reported salicin for acute rheumatism in The Lancet, and salicylates became standard therapy, limited by gastric irritation and nausea.

**The 1897 modification.** Charles Gerhardt had made crude acetylsalicylic acid in 1853 but did not pursue it. At Bayer, a dye company that had opened a pharmaceutical division in 1888, Felix Hoffmann reacted salicylic acid with **acetic anhydride**, giving a pure, stable product. Key points:
- Pharmacology chief **Heinrich Dreser** was reportedly skeptical at first, worried about effects on the heart, and was more enthusiastic about another acetylated product Hoffmann made eleven days later, diacetylmorphine, sold from 1898 as Heroin.
- Clinical reports in 1899 were favorable, and Bayer trademarked **Aspirin** on 6 March 1899.
- Germany refused a patent because the compound had been made before; the US granted one in 1900, which expired in 1917.

**Losing the name.** After World War I, wartime seizures and the 1919 **Treaty of Versailles** stripped Bayer of the Aspirin trademark in countries including the US, Britain and France. Sterling Drug bought Bayer's US assets in 1918, and in 1921 Judge **Learned Hand** ruled that 'aspirin' had become a generic word for American consumers.

Remarkably, for more than 70 years nobody knew how aspirin actually worked.
levels.phd:
**Mechanism, found late.** In 1971 **John Vane** (Nature) showed that aspirin and related drugs block **prostaglandin synthesis**. That work earned him a share of the 1982 Nobel Prize with Sune Bergström and Bengt Samuelsson. In 1975 **Roth and Majerus** showed that aspirin donates its acetyl group to platelet cyclooxygenase. The target residue was later mapped to **Ser530** of COX-1 (prostaglandin H synthase-1), and the 1995 crystal structure of acetylated COX-1 (Loll, Picot and Garavito) explained the result. The acetylated serine sits in the hydrophobic channel and sterically blocks arachidonic acid from reaching the cyclooxygenase site. The inhibition is **covalent and irreversible**, unlike the competitive, reversible binding of most NSAIDs.

**Why platelets are special.** Platelets are anucleate and cannot make new COX-1. A single exposure abolishes **thromboxane A2** production for the platelet's lifespan (about 7-10 days). Endothelial cells resynthesize COX and recover **prostacyclin** (PGI2) production. This difference underlies the antithrombotic effect.

Aspirin is hydrolyzed by plasma and liver esterases to salicylate within minutes. Much platelet acetylation occurs **presystemically**, in portal blood, before aspirin reaches the systemic circulation.

**COX-2 is modified, not silenced.** Acetylation of COX-2 (Ser516) switches the enzyme to make **15(R)-HETE**. Leukocyte 5-lipoxygenase converts this to **aspirin-triggered lipoxins** (15-epi-LXA4). Charles Serhan's group showed these are pro-resolving mediators. COX-2 itself was only identified around 1991.

**Salicylate's own pharmacology.** Salicylic acid barely inhibits purified COX in vitro, yet it is anti-inflammatory in vivo. Proposed mechanisms include suppression of COX-2 transcription, inhibition of IKK-beta/NF-kB signaling, and direct activation of AMPK. In plants, salicylic acid is a defense hormone, which hints at why willow makes it at all.

**Historiographic controversy.** Arthur Eichengrün, Hoffmann's supervisor, claimed in 1949 that he had planned the synthesis. He wrote after Nazi-era persecution, as a Jewish chemist imprisoned at Theresienstadt, that had erased his role. The famous story that Hoffmann acted to help his rheumatic father first appeared in a 1934 footnote. Walter Sneader's 2000 BMJ reappraisal found Eichengrün's account credible. Bayer disputes this, and the attribution remains contested.
levels.expert:
Aspirin's second life as a cardiovascular drug began with **Lawrence Craven**, a California general practitioner. In the late 1940s he noticed unusual bleeding in tonsillectomy patients chewing aspirin gum. He then recommended aspirin to thousands of men and claimed in the 1950s that almost none had heart attacks. His studies were uncontrolled and largely ignored.

The decisive evidence came from **ISIS-2** (1988). Aspirin given in suspected acute MI cut 5-week vascular mortality by about 23%, and the benefit added to streptokinase. Secondary prevention became standard.

**Primary prevention reversed.** ASPREE, ASCEND and ARRIVE (all 2018) showed modest or absent net benefit once major bleeding was counted. ASPREE, in older adults, even found higher all-cause mortality, mostly from cancer. In 2022 the USPSTF advised against starting aspirin for primary prevention at age 60 or older.

**Pitfalls clinicians watch:**
- **Ibuprofen interaction**: taken first, ibuprofen occupies the COX-1 channel and blocks aspirin from reaching Ser530 (FDA advisory, 2006).
- **Variable response**: enteric coating and higher body weight are linked to weaker platelet inhibition. Rothwell's 2018 Lancet analysis suggested one fixed regimen does not fit all patients.
- **Reye syndrome**: an epidemiological link with aspirin in children with viral illness led to 1980s warnings, and cases fell sharply afterward.
- **Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease** (Samter's triad of asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity). COX-1 blockade shunts arachidonic acid toward cysteinyl leukotrienes.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Because inhibition is irreversible, platelet function recovers only as new platelets are produced, about 10% per day. Aspirin is therefore often held for roughly a week before elective cranial or spinal surgery. That benefit is weighed against stent thrombosis or stroke risk, and platelet function assays can guide timing. Giving fresh platelets looked like a logical fix for antiplatelet-associated spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage. In practice, the **PATCH trial** (2016) found platelet transfusion was associated with worse functional outcome.

**Open questions.** In **CAPP2**, aspirin reduced colorectal cancer in Lynch syndrome carriers. Who should take aspirin for cancer prevention, and how much of that effect is COX-independent, remain unresolved. A 19th-century molecule is still generating trials.

lessons.title: Chloral Hydrate and Barbital: The First Synthetic Sedatives

levels.kid:
Long ago, doctors had very few ways to help people who could not sleep or who felt very upset. Most medicines came from plants, like poppies or willow trees.

Then chemists learned to build brand-new molecules in their labs, a bit like snapping Lego bricks together.

In 1869, a German doctor named Oscar Liebreich tried a lab-made chemical called **chloral hydrate**. It helped people fall asleep quickly. It was one of the first sleep medicines made by people instead of plants.

In 1903, two scientists, Emil Fischer and Joseph von Mering, made **barbital**. Its calming effect lasted a long time. It was the first member of a big medicine family called **barbiturates**.

These medicines helped many people. But too much could be very dangerous, so doctors had to be very careful.
levels.hs:
A **sedative** calms a person. A **hypnotic** (named after Hypnos, the Greek god of sleep) brings on sleep. Many drugs do both, depending on how much is given. Before the 1860s doctors relied mostly on opium, alcohol and **bromide salts**. Chloral hydrate and barbital were among the first **synthetic** medicines: molecules built by chemists rather than taken from nature.

**Chloral hydrate.** The German chemist **Justus von Liebig** first made it in 1832 by chlorinating ethanol. In 1869 the Berlin pharmacologist **Oscar Liebreich** tested it as a sleep drug. His reasoning was that blood is slightly alkaline, so the drug should break down into **chloroform**, a known anesthetic. The drug worked, but his explanation was wrong. The body actually converts it into **trichloroethanol**, which does the real work.

**Barbital.** In 1864 **Adolf von Baeyer** made **barbituric acid** from urea and malonic acid. It has no sedative effect. In 1903 **Emil Fischer** and **Joseph von Mering** showed that adding two ethyl groups created a strong hypnotic, **barbital**, sold by Bayer from 1904 as **Veronal**.

Both drugs calm neurons by boosting **GABA**, the brain's main inhibitory messenger. Their great weakness was a **narrow therapeutic index**: the amount that sedates is not far from the amount that stops breathing. Dependence and dangerous withdrawal were also common, so from the 1960s **benzodiazepines** largely replaced them.
levels.college:
The late 1800s saw a run of synthetic sedative-hypnotics, each an improvement on unreliable plant extracts:
- **Bromides** (Locock, 1857): simple inorganic salts, slow to clear and prone to chronic toxicity (bromism).
- **Chloral hydrate** (Liebreich, 1869): the first synthetic organic hypnotic.
- **Paraldehyde** (1882) and **sulfonal** (Baumann and Kast, 1888).
- **Barbital** (Fischer and von Mering, 1903), launched as Veronal in 1904; **phenobarbital** (Luminal) followed in 1912.

**Chloral chemistry.** Chloral is trichloroacetaldehyde (CCl3CHO). The strongly electron-withdrawing CCl3 group makes the aldehyde carbon so electrophilic that it forms a stable **gem-diol**, CCl3CH(OH)2, the hydrate. In the body, alcohol dehydrogenase reduces it to **trichloroethanol**, the main active hypnotic. Some is oxidized to **trichloroacetic acid**, a long-lived but largely inactive metabolite.

**Barbiturate structure-activity.** Barbituric acid is a pyrimidine ring with no CNS activity. Hypnotic activity needs **two substituents at carbon 5**. Barbital carries two ethyl groups there. Larger or branched groups raise lipid solubility, speeding brain entry and liver metabolism. Swapping the C2 oxygen for sulfur gives thiobarbiturates such as thiopental, which act within seconds.

Lipid solubility set the classic duration classes:
- Long-acting: barbital, phenobarbital
- Short-acting: pentobarbital, secobarbital
- Ultrashort-acting: thiopental, ended mainly by redistribution out of the brain into muscle and fat

**Mechanism.** Both drug families are positive modulators of the **GABA-A receptor**, a chloride channel. Barbiturates **prolong each channel opening**, whereas benzodiazepines increase how often it opens. More chloride entering makes neurons harder to fire.

**Problems.** Narrow therapeutic index, respiratory depression, tolerance, physical dependence and severe withdrawal, sometimes with seizures. Phenobarbital also strongly induces liver enzymes, causing many drug interactions.
levels.phd:
**Liebreich's hypothesis** is an early example of prodrug reasoning. He predicted that chloral would undergo a haloform-type cleavage in alkaline blood, releasing chloroform. No meaningful chloroform forms at physiological pH. In 1948 T. C. Butler identified **trichloroethanol** (TCE) as the active hypnotic, formed by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) using NADH. TCE is then glucuronidated (urochloralic acid) and excreted. The drug succeeded despite a wrong mechanism.

The classic **ethanol interaction** follows from this shared biochemistry. Oxidizing ethanol raises hepatic NADH, which speeds reduction of chloral to TCE. TCE in turn inhibits ethanol oxidation. Both sedatives therefore rise together, a pharmacokinetic synergy on top of their additive effects at GABA-A receptors.

**Barbiturate SAR** was mapped empirically within a decade of barbital. C5 disubstitution is required. Hypnotic potency rises with total C5 carbon count up to a plateau, beyond which convulsant activity can appear. N-methylation and C2 sulfur both increase lipophilicity. Barbital's pKa is about 7.9, so it is largely un-ionized in plasma. Being poorly metabolized, it is cleared slowly and largely unchanged by the kidney, which explains its long action and next-day hangover.

**Receptor pharmacology.** Single-channel recordings by Twyman, Rogers and Macdonald (1989) showed that barbiturates increase mean open time by favoring longer-lived open states. Diazepam instead raises opening frequency. Cryo-EM structures (Kim, Hibbs and colleagues, 2020) placed phenobarbital in transmembrane pockets at subunit interfaces, distinct from the benzodiazepine site at the extracellular α+/γ− interface. Two further actions explain the lethality:
- At higher concentrations barbiturates **gate the channel directly**, with no GABA present, so there is no ceiling effect.
- They also inhibit AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors.

Benzodiazepines need endogenous GABA, which caps their effect when taken alone.

**Enzyme induction.** Phenobarbital activates the nuclear receptor CAR, inducing CYP2B, CYP3A and others. It also induces **ALA synthase**, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis. This is why barbiturates can trigger attacks of acute intermittent porphyria.
levels.expert:
Neither drug is a museum piece, and neurosurgery is where barbiturates matter most today.

**Barbiturate coma.** Pentobarbital lowers cerebral metabolic rate for oxygen (CMRO2). Through flow-metabolism coupling, this reduces cerebral blood volume and intracranial pressure. It is titrated to **EEG burst suppression**. Eisenberg's 1988 randomized trial showed better ICP control in refractory cases. Cochrane reviews, however, find no convincing improvement in mortality or functional outcome. Barbiturate-induced hypotension can cut cerebral perfusion pressure and cancel the benefit. Current guidelines keep it as a tier-3 option for refractory intracranial hypertension. Pitfalls include prolonged accumulation, which confounds brain-death testing, along with immunosuppression and the need for invasive hemodynamic monitoring.

**Phenobarbital's revival.**
- **Neonatal seizures:** the NEOLEV2 trial (Sharpe et al., 2020) found phenobarbital substantially more effective than levetiracetam as first-line therapy. This reversed a trend driven by fears about phenobarbital-related neuronal apoptosis seen in developing animal brains.
- **Alcohol withdrawal:** phenobarbital protocols are increasingly used, especially when benzodiazepines fail.
- Its long half-life smooths levels but makes toxicity slow to resolve. Urinary alkalinization and multidose activated charcoal can speed its clearance.

**Chloral hydrate today.** It was long used for pediatric sedation during EEG, echocardiography and imaging, but use has fallen sharply:
- The FDA's action against unapproved marketed drugs led US manufacturers to stop production around 2012.
- Delayed or prolonged sedation has been reported after discharge.
- At toxic levels it sensitizes the myocardium to catecholamines and can cause ventricular arrhythmias.
- IARC classifies chloral hydrate as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A). It also forms as a byproduct when drinking water is chlorinated.
- Its metabolite trichloroacetic acid displaces warfarin from albumin.

**Lessons and open questions.** These drugs taught pharmacology that efficacy without selectivity is not enough. The modern goal is subtype-selective GABA-A modulators, such as α2/α3-preferring agents for anxiety without sedation, and extrasynaptic δ-subunit targets such as neurosteroids. Success has been mixed. Why some anesthetic-site ligands depress breathing far more than others remains only partly explained.

Liebreich wrongly thought it released chloroform; trichloroethanol is the active metabolite
Barbituric acid (Baeyer 1864) is inactive; barbital (Fischer and von Mering 1903) needs two C5 groups
Barbiturates prolong GABA-A chloride channel opening and can open it directly at high levels
Narrow therapeutic index, dependence and dangerous withdrawal led benzodiazepines to replace them
Legacy uses: pentobarbital coma for refractory ICP, phenobarbital for neonatal seizures

lessons.title: Ehrlich's Magic Bullet: Salvarsan Against Syphilis (1910)

levels.kid:
Imagine a medicine that works like a key. It fits only one lock, the lock on a germ. It opens that lock and stops the germ, but it does not fit the locks on your own body. A scientist named **Paul Ehrlich** dreamed of medicines like that. He called them **magic bullets**.

Ehrlich noticed that some colorful dyes stuck to certain germs and not to others. So he thought: why not make chemicals that stick to germs and hurt them?

His team made hundreds of new chemicals. Number **606** worked against a serious germ disease called **syphilis**. It was called **Salvarsan**. It was not perfect, but it showed that scientists could build germ-fighting medicines on purpose.
levels.hs:
In 1910, the German scientist **Paul Ehrlich** announced the first modern drug designed to kill a specific microbe inside the body. It was called **Salvarsan**, and it treated **syphilis**, a sexually transmitted infection caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium, **Treponema pallidum**. Untreated syphilis can damage the heart and brain years later.

Before Salvarsan, the main treatment was **mercury**, which was toxic and worked poorly.

Ehrlich's big idea came from dyes. He saw that certain dyes stained some cells and microbes but not others. If a chemical could stick to a germ selectively, perhaps it could kill the germ while sparing the patient. He called this ideal drug a **magic bullet** and named the field **chemotherapy**, meaning chemicals used to attack disease-causing organisms.

How Salvarsan was found:
- His team started from **Atoxyl**, an arsenic compound that was active against some parasites but could damage the optic nerve and cause blindness.
- Chemist **Alfred Bertheim** made hundreds of arsenic variations.
- In 1909, Japanese scientist **Sahachiro Hata** tested them in rabbits infected with syphilis. Compound **606** worked dramatically.

Salvarsan was given by injection into a vein. It had real side effects, and an easier version, **Neosalvarsan**, followed in 1912. Penicillin replaced both in the 1940s.
levels.college:
Salvarsan (**arsphenamine**) was the first rationally pursued synthetic antimicrobial, and it established the method of modern drug discovery: make many related compounds, test them in an animal disease model, and pick the one with the best balance of effectiveness and toxicity.

**Ehrlich's intellectual foundations**
- **Selective staining**: as a student, Ehrlich used aniline dyes to distinguish cell types. In 1891 he and Paul Guttmann treated malaria patients with **methylene blue**, a dye that stains the malaria parasite.
- **Side-chain theory** (1897–1900): cells carry chemical "side chains" that bind specific substances. This became an early form of the **receptor** concept, summarized in his phrase *corpora non agunt nisi fixata* ("substances do not act unless they are bound").
- With Kiyoshi Shiga he found **trypan red** active against trypanosomes in mice (1904).

**From Atoxyl to 606**
Atoxyl, first made by Antoine Béchamp in 1859, was shown in 1905 to kill trypanosomes. Ehrlich and Bertheim showed its true structure was **arsanilic acid**, with a free amino group that could be chemically modified. That opened the door to systematic derivatives. Fritz Schaudinn and Erich Hoffmann had identified the syphilis spirochete in 1905, and the **Wassermann blood test** (1906) offered a way to track infection. Compound 606, made in 1907, was first judged inactive; Hata's rabbit syphilis model in 1909 revealed its power.

**Launch and problems**
- Announced in April 1910; Hoechst marketed it that year.
- It oxidized in air, becoming more toxic, so it was sealed in ampoules and had to be dissolved and neutralized before intravenous injection.
- Adverse effects included vein irritation, liver damage, nerve injury and occasional deaths.
- Patients could develop the **Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction**: fever and worsening rash hours after treatment, from products released by dying spirochetes.

**Neosalvarsan** (compound 914, 1912) was more soluble and simpler to give. Arsenicals remained standard until penicillin.
levels.phd:
Ehrlich's program is the founding case study of **chemotherapy as selective toxicity**. His working metric was the **chemotherapeutic index**: the ratio of the maximum tolerated dose to the minimum curative dose. A high index means a wide margin between cure and host toxicity. This is a conceptual ancestor of the modern therapeutic index.

**Structure-guided derivatization.** Béchamp had misassigned Atoxyl as an anilide. Ehrlich and Bertheim (1907) showed it was sodium arsanilate, carrying a free aromatic amine. This reactive handle, along with reduction of pentavalent arsenic (As^V) to trivalent arsenic (As^III), allowed the synthesis of hundreds of analogues. Ehrlich reasoned, correctly, that trivalent arsenicals were the more parasiticidal species. Pentavalent Atoxyl acted largely after being reduced inside the body.

The number "606" is usually described as the 606th compound tested. In fact it was a laboratory serial designation, and the popular story simplifies the series. The compound's early dismissal illustrates a durable lesson: screening outcomes depend on the model. Mouse trypanosomiasis did not predict activity against treponemes, but Hata's rabbit model of syphilitic orchitis and chancre did.

**Mechanism.** Trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups, especially **vicinal dithiols** in proteins and cofactors such as lipoamide in pyruvate dehydrogenase. Carl Voegtlin's work in the 1920s supported the view that arsphenamine is oxidized in vivo to an **arsenoxide** (oxophenarsine, later sold as Mapharsen), which is the active species. Salvarsan thus behaves as a **prodrug**. The precise treponemal target was never defined, partly because T. pallidum could not be grown in culture.

**Structure controversy.** For nearly a century textbooks drew Salvarsan as a dimer with an As=As double bond, by analogy with azo dyes. In 2005, Lloyd, Morgan, Nicholson and colleagues used electrospray mass spectrometry to show it is a mixture of cyclic **trimers (As3) and pentamers (As5)** joined by As–As single bonds. These rings are consistent with slow oxidative release of the active arsenoxide.

**Resistance.** Ehrlich documented "arsenic-fast" trypanosome strains and showed that resistance was specific to particular chemical classes. This was one of the first experimental demonstrations of acquired drug resistance and of cross-resistance patterns.
levels.expert:
Salvarsan's clinical life was turbulent and instructive. Toxicity reports, deaths, and accusations of profiteering against Hoechst fed a public campaign against Ehrlich, culminating in a 1914 libel trial in Frankfurt. The episode foreshadowed modern tensions over post-marketing safety, drug pricing and the use of vulnerable patients in early testing, including controversial trials on prostitutes in state hospitals. There was still no regulatory framework requiring controlled trials. Batch variability was a real hazard: each lot was tested for toxicity in animals before release, an early form of biological standardization.

**The neurological dimension.** Late syphilis caused **general paresis** and **tabes dorsalis**, which filled asylums. Arsenicals penetrated the central nervous system poorly, so neurosyphilis responded unreliably. This gap led Julius Wagner-Jauregg to deliberately induce malarial fevers to treat paresis (Nobel Prize, 1927). Tryparsamide, a pentavalent arsenical with better CNS penetration, was also used. For a future neurosurgeon, the lesson is that blood–brain barrier penetration can decide whether a systemically "curative" drug works in the nervous system.

**Replacement.** In 1943, John Mahoney and colleagues at the US Marine Hospital on Staten Island cured early syphilis with penicillin. Prolonged arsenical courses gave way rapidly to a far safer drug. Penicillin remains first-line today, and recurring shortages of long-acting benzathine penicillin, amid a resurgence of syphilis including congenital cases, are a current public health concern.

**Arsenic's afterlife in medicine:**
- **Melarsoprol** was long the treatment for late-stage gambiense sleeping sickness, despite causing a fatal reactive encephalopathy in a minority of patients. In T. brucei, loss of the aquaglyceroporin **AQP2** mediates melarsoprol–pentamidine cross-resistance, a molecular echo of Ehrlich's arsenic-fast strains. Nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy and oral **fexinidazole** have now largely displaced it.
- **Arsenic trioxide** induces degradation of the PML–RARA fusion protein and, combined with all-trans retinoic acid, cures most cases of acute promyelocytic leukemia. It is a genuine targeted therapy built on Ehrlich's element.

**Open questions.** The treponemal target of arsphenamine remains unknown. The 2005 cyclic-oligomer structure invites renewed study of how prodrug release kinetics shaped both efficacy and toxicity. Ehrlich's receptor-based selectivity concept still frames antibody–drug conjugates, which are literal magic bullets.

lessons.title: Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod Discover Insulin (1921–22)

levels.kid:
Long ago, if a child got a sickness called **diabetes**, doctors could not fix it. The child's body could not use the sugar from food, so the sugar piled up in the blood. Sadly, most of these children died.

In 1921, in Toronto, Canada, a young doctor named **Frederick Banting** and a student named **Charles Best** had an idea. A body part called the **pancreas** makes a special messenger called **insulin**. Insulin works like a key that unlocks cells so sugar can get inside and be used for energy.

A chemist named **James Collip** cleaned up their pancreas juice so it was safe. Their boss, **John Macleod**, guided the work. In 1922, a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson got the medicine and got much better. Families everywhere called it a miracle!
levels.hs:
Before 1922, **type 1 diabetes** was a death sentence, often within a year or two for children. The body could not control **blood glucose** (sugar), so sugar spilled into the urine, and the body burned fat so fast that acids called **ketones** built up and poisoned the blood. The best treatment was a near-starvation diet that only bought time.

The big clue came in 1889, when Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering removed a dog's pancreas and the dog developed diabetes. Scientists suspected that the **islets of Langerhans**, small clusters of cells in the pancreas, released a **hormone** (a chemical messenger carried in the blood) that controlled sugar. But attempts to extract it kept failing.

In 1920, **Frederick Banting**, a young surgeon in London, Ontario, proposed tying off the pancreas's ducts so the enzyme-making tissue would waste away, leaving the islets to extract. Professor **John J. R. Macleod** at the University of Toronto gave him lab space, dogs and a student assistant, **Charles Best**. In summer 1921, their extracts lowered blood sugar in dogs with no pancreas.

Biochemist **James Collip** then purified the extract. A crude injection given to 14-year-old **Leonard Thompson** on January 11, 1922, largely failed, but Collip's purified version on January 23 dramatically lowered his blood sugar and ketones.

In 1923, Banting and Macleod won the Nobel Prize. Banting shared his prize money with Best, and Macleod shared his with Collip. The discoverers sold their patent to the university for one dollar each so insulin could be made widely.
levels.college:
**Insulin** is a peptide hormone made by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets. It lowers blood glucose by driving glucose into muscle and fat cells (via the **GLUT4** transporter), promoting glycogen storage, and suppressing glucose output from the liver. It also restrains lipolysis and **ketogenesis**, which is why its absence produces diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Why earlier extracts failed.** The pancreas is mostly exocrine tissue full of digestive enzymes. When ground up, enzymes such as **trypsin** can digest a protein hormone. Crude extracts also contained impurities that caused fever and abscesses, and nobody yet expected that an effective extract could drop blood sugar dangerously low.

**Banting's rationale.** After reading Moses Barron's 1920 report that a blocked pancreatic duct caused the enzyme-producing acinar tissue to atrophy while the islets survived, Banting wrote down his plan on October 31, 1920: ligate the ducts, wait for the acini to degenerate, then extract the islets.

Key steps:
- **May 1921:** Banting and Best begin work in Macleod's Toronto laboratory.
- **Summer to autumn 1921:** extracts of degenerated pancreas lower blood glucose in depancreatized dogs; one dog, Marjorie, is kept alive about ten weeks. The team moves to fetal calf, then whole adult beef pancreas.
- **December 1921:** Collip joins and develops **fractional alcohol precipitation**, finding the alcohol concentrations at which impurities drop out and the active principle can be isolated.
- **January 1922:** Leonard Thompson is treated successfully with Collip's extract.
- **1922:** Eli Lilly and Company partners with Toronto; Lilly chemist George Walden's isoelectric precipitation greatly improves purity and yield, and by 1923 insulin is widely available.

Macleod suggested the name "insulin" (from the Latin *insula*, island), which had earlier been proposed by Jean de Meyer and Edward Sharpey-Schafer. Measuring blood glucose, urine glucose and urinary ketones gave the team objective evidence that their extract worked.
levels.phd:
The insulin story is a case study in how scientific credit is assigned. Several investigators came close before Toronto. Georg Zuelzer treated patients with a pancreatic extract (Acomatol) from 1908 but stopped because of toxic reactions. Ernest Scott (1911) and Israel Kleiner (1919) reported glucose-lowering effects in animals. Most pointedly, the Romanian physiologist **Nicolae Paulescu** published in August 1921 that his "pancréine" lowered blood glucose and ketones in depancreatized dogs. Toronto's claim to priority rests on producing the first extract shown to be safe and effective in human patients, and on making it reproducible and scalable.

Ironically, Banting's founding hypothesis was not needed. Duct ligation to remove acinar enzymes proved dispensable once the team extracted whole beef pancreas in **acidified alcohol**, conditions that inhibit trypsin and denature many contaminating proteins. The decisive advances were biochemical (Collip's purification) and physiological (Macleod's rigor), not the surgical idea.

Collip's work also revealed a key danger. Testing extracts in normal rabbits, he saw blood glucose fall until the animals convulsed, and found that glucose reversed the convulsions. This established **hypoglycemia** as insulin's main acute toxicity and gave a **rabbit bioassay**: early units were defined by their effect on fasted rabbits, a way to standardize potency between batches.

The team was deeply divided. Banting distrusted Macleod and resented Collip; at one point he reportedly assaulted Collip when Collip seemed unwilling to share his method. Collip temporarily lost the ability to reproduce his purification in spring 1922. When the 1923 Nobel Prize went to Banting and Macleod, less than two years after the first patient was treated, both shared the money with the collaborator they felt had been overlooked. August Krogh, the Danish Nobel laureate who visited Toronto in 1922 and championed the work, helped bring insulin to Scandinavia.

Michael Bliss's 1982 history, *The Discovery of Insulin*, reassessed the popular "Banting and Best" story and restored credit to Collip and Macleod as part of a team effort. Insulin later became a molecular landmark: John Jacob Abel crystallized it in 1926, and Frederick Sanger's 1955 sequence made it the first protein ever sequenced.
levels.expert:
Early insulin solved one problem and exposed several more. Animal-derived insulin had a short action, which forced patients to take multiple injections a day. That drove a series of formulation advances: Hans Christian Hagedorn's **protamine insulin** (1936), David Scott's **zinc insulin** work (1934) and **NPH** insulin (1946), each slowing absorption from the injection site. Bovine and porcine preparations also contained contaminants that caused lipoatrophy at injection sites and allergic reactions.

Immunogenicity proved scientifically fertile. In the 1950s, Solomon Berson and **Rosalyn Yalow** showed that patients treated with insulin developed antibodies that bound it. They turned that binding into **radioimmunoassay** (RIA), letting scientists measure tiny hormone concentrations in blood for the first time; Yalow received the 1977 Nobel Prize. In 1967, Donald Steiner discovered **proinsulin**, showing that insulin is cut from a single-chain precursor. This gave clinicians **C-peptide**, released in matching amounts, as a marker of a patient's own insulin secretion. It is useful for telling type 1 from type 2 diabetes and for detecting surreptitious insulin use as a cause of hypoglycemia. Dorothy Hodgkin solved insulin's 3D structure in 1969.

In 1982, **recombinant human insulin** (Humulin, from Genentech and Lilly) became the first recombinant DNA drug approved. Engineered analogues followed: insulin lispro (1996) speeds absorption by swapping two amino acids, and glargine prolongs action. These are examples of designing a hormone's pharmacokinetics at the sequence level.

For a future neurosurgeon, the lesson Collip learned in rabbits still matters. The brain depends on a steady glucose supply, so **neuroglycopenia** can cause confusion, seizures and coma. In neurocritical care, both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia worsen outcomes after brain injury, so glucose targets are deliberately moderate.

The current frontier aims to replace or protect beta cells rather than the hormone:
- **Teplizumab** (FDA, 2022), an anti-CD3 antibody, delays the onset of clinical type 1 diabetes.
- **Donislecel** (Lantidra, 2023), from deceased donors, is the first FDA-approved allogeneic islet cell therapy.
- Stem-cell-derived islet trials have made some patients insulin-independent.

Open questions include avoiding lifelong immunosuppression after cell therapy. Insulin access is another: a century after the one-dollar patent, cost remains a barrier for many patients, an ironic echo of the founders' intentions.

keyPoints: Before 1922, type 1 diabetes was fatal; starvation diets only bought time
Minkowski and von Mering (1889) linked the pancreas to diabetes
Banting and Best's 1921 dog experiments in Macleod's Toronto lab showed extracts lowered blood sugar
Collip's purification made the first safe, effective human treatment (Leonard Thompson, January 1922)
1923 Nobel Prize to Banting and Macleod, who shared it with Best and Collip; patent sold for $1 each
Insulin's legacy: hypoglycemia risk, radioimmunoassay, recombinant insulin, and modern cell therapies

test.q: In 1889, Minkowski and von Mering showed that removing a dog's pancreas causes:
test.explain: Removing the pancreas caused diabetes, pointing to a pancreatic substance that controls blood sugar.

test.q: What was James Collip's main contribution to the insulin work?
test.explain: Collip, a biochemist, used fractional alcohol precipitation to purify the extract enough for safe use in patients. The duct-ligation idea was Banting's.

test.q: Why did Banting want to tie off the pancreatic ducts before making an extract?
choices: To boost acid secretion in the stomach
To let enzyme-making tissue waste away
To make the islets grow larger and faster
To stop the hormone leaking into the gut
test.explain: Ligation causes the enzyme-producing acinar tissue to atrophy, which Banting hoped would stop digestive enzymes from destroying the islet hormone.

test.q: Leonard Thompson's first injection on January 11, 1922 largely failed mainly because the extract was:
test.explain: The crude extract was impure, causing an abscess and only a modest effect. Collip's purified extract on January 23 worked dramatically.

test.q: The 1923 Nobel Prize for the discovery of insulin was awarded to:
test.explain: The prize went to Banting and Macleod. Banting shared his money with Best, and Macleod shared his with Collip.

test.q: Insulin lowers blood glucose mainly by:
choices: Blocking glucose absorption from the gut
Pushing glucose out through the kidneys
Breaking down glucose in the bloodstream
Driving glucose into muscle and fat cells
test.explain: Insulin increases glucose uptake into muscle and fat (via GLUT4), promotes glycogen storage, and suppresses liver glucose output.

test.q: Why did many earlier pancreatic extracts fail?
choices: Insulin is destroyed by cold storage
Digestive enzymes broke down the hormone
The islets make no hormone in adults
Animal hormones fail to act in humans
test.explain: The pancreas is full of enzymes like trypsin that can digest a protein hormone. Impurities that caused fevers and abscesses were another problem.

test.q: For what did the discoverers sell the insulin patent to the University of Toronto?
test.explain: They sold it for one dollar each so insulin could be produced widely rather than for personal profit.

test.q: Which company partnered with Toronto in 1922 to mass-produce insulin?
test.explain: Eli Lilly partnered with Toronto, and Lilly chemist George Walden's isoelectric precipitation greatly improved purity and yield.

test.q: Which organ contains the beta cells that make insulin?
test.explain: Insulin is made by beta cells in the islets of the pancreas.

test.q: The hormone-producing cell clusters in the pancreas are called the islets of ___.
test.explain: The islets of Langerhans are the endocrine clusters that release insulin.

test.q: Which University of Toronto physiology professor gave Banting lab space, dogs and a student assistant?
test.explain: J. J. R. Macleod, a carbohydrate metabolism expert, supported and guided the work and later shared the Nobel Prize.

kidTest.q: What does insulin do in the body?
kidTest.explain: Insulin works like a key that lets sugar into cells to be used for energy.

kidTest.q: In which city was insulin discovered?
kidTest.explain: Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod worked in Toronto, Canada.

kidTest.q: Who cleaned up the pancreas juice so it was safe to use?
kidTest.explain: James Collip was the chemist who purified the medicine.

kidTest.q: How old was Leonard Thompson when he got insulin?
kidTest.explain: Leonard was a 14-year-old boy, and insulin helped him get better.

kidTest.q: Which body part makes insulin? p _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: The pancreas makes insulin.

advancedTest.q: Later work showed Banting's duct-ligation step was unnecessary. The best explanation is that:
choices: Duct-ligated dogs made more insulin than normal dogs
Acid-alcohol extraction kept trypsin from destroying it
Fetal tissue lacked islets, so atrophy did not matter
Insulin proved to come from acinar cells, not islets
advancedTest.explain: Extracting whole pancreas in acidified alcohol inhibits trypsin and removes contaminants, so atrophying the acini first was not needed.

advancedTest.q: Thompson's first extract lowered glucose only modestly, ketones persisted and an abscess formed; Collip's extract then cleared his ketonuria. This mainly shows that:
choices: Contaminants, not lack of hormone, limited the first extract
Ketone clearance needs a hormone separate from glucose control
An abscess is a reliable sign that an extract is effective
His diabetes had remitted in the twelve days between doses
advancedTest.explain: The same hormone was present in both extracts; purification removed impurities and allowed the full effect, including suppression of ketogenesis.

advancedTest.q: Why is Toronto credited over Paulescu, despite Paulescu's August 1921 report of glucose-lowering in dogs?
choices: Paulescu's extract had no effect on blood sugar in dogs
Toronto filed a patent before Paulescu began his work
Paulescu published his work after the Nobel announcement
Toronto first made an extract proven to work in patients
advancedTest.explain: Paulescu did show effects in dogs. Toronto's priority rests on the first safe, effective, reproducible human treatment and its scale-up.

advancedTest.q: Berson and Yalow's finding of insulin-binding antibodies in treated patients was pivotal mainly because it:
choices: Led to radioimmunoassay for measuring tiny hormone levels
Showed that animal insulin has no effect in human patients
Explained why oral insulin is digested in the stomach
Proved that type 1 diabetes is caused by a viral infection
advancedTest.explain: Turning antibody binding into a measurement tool gave radioimmunoassay, earning Yalow the 1977 Nobel Prize. Animal insulin did work in humans despite the antibodies.
